## The running example (for reference)

| | |
|---|---|
| **P** — Population | Adults (18+) with septic shock in the ICU |
| **I** — Intervention | Restrictive fluid strategy |
| **C** — Comparison | Usual care (standard fluids) |
| **O** — Outcome | Death from any cause |
| **T** — Time | Within 28 days |

**Question:** *In adults with septic shock in the ICU, does a restrictive fluid strategy, compared with usual care, reduce 28-day mortality?*

## Exercise 1 — Boolean search builder  *(individual, 5 minutes, segment 2.1)*

**Rules:** synonyms inside a block are joined with **OR**; blocks are joined with **AND**; put each block in **brackets**. Write operators in CAPITALS. Use English search words.

**Warm-up — which gives MORE hits?** (circle)
- `septic shock AND fluids`  or  `septic shock OR fluids`
- `sepsis`  or  `sepsis NOT neonatal`

**Build your search** from your group's PICO question (Session 1) and your synonym list. The comparison (C) is usually *not* searched.

| Block | Concept | Synonyms (2–4). Mark possible MeSH terms with (M) |
|---|---|---|
| **P** | | |
| **I / E** | | |
| **O** | | |

**My search string:**

`( ______ OR ______ OR ______ ) AND ( ______ OR ______ OR ______ ) AND ( ______ OR ______ )`

**One filter I would add, and why:** __________________________________________

**Swap with your neighbour.** One synonym they suggest adding: ______________________

**The search string from the live demo (copy it here to run at home):**

```
("Shock, Septic"[Mesh] OR "septic shock"[tiab] OR sepsis[tiab])
AND ("Fluid Therapy"[Mesh] OR "fluid restrict*"[tiab] OR "restrictive fluid*"[tiab] OR "conservative fluid*"[tiab])
AND ("Mortality"[Mesh] OR mortality[tiab] OR death[tiab])
```

| Field tag / symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `[Mesh]` or `[mh]` | MeSH term (includes narrower terms automatically) |
| `[tiab]` | word in the title or abstract |
| `[pt]` | publication type, e.g. `randomized controlled trial[pt]` |
| `"..."` | exact phrase |
| `*` | any ending (truncation): `restrict*` = restrict, restricted, restriction, restrictive |

## Exercise 2 — Citing vs copying: paraphrase safely  *(individual, at home, 10 minutes)*

**Method:** read → close the paper → write from memory → check the facts → cite.
Patchwriting (copying the sentence and swapping a few words) is plagiarism **even with a reference**.

**Part A — Spot the problem.** The source is the Results section of Paper 2's abstract (Hyun 2023):

> "The positive fluid groups in both the D2 (HR, 2.13; 95% CI 1.48–3.06; P < 0.001) and D3 (HR, 1.56; 95% CI 1.10–2.22; P = 0.012) cohorts had significantly higher mortality rates than the negative fluid groups."

For each version, tick **OK** or **Problem**, and say why.

| Version | OK | Problem | Why? |
|---|---|---|---|
| a) "The positive fluid groups in the D2 and D3 cohorts had significantly higher death rates than the negative fluid groups [2]." | ☐ | ☐ | |
| b) "In a matched registry cohort, a positive cumulative fluid balance on ICU days 2 and 3 was associated with higher 28-day mortality (hazard ratios 2.13 and 1.56) [2]." | ☐ | ☐ | |
| c) "Giving more fluid on days 2 and 3 doubles the risk of death [2]." | ☐ | ☐ | |
| d) "In a matched registry cohort, a positive cumulative fluid balance on ICU days 2 and 3 was associated with higher 28-day mortality." (no citation) | ☐ | ☐ | |

**Part B — Your turn.** Paraphrase this sentence from Paper 1's abstract in your own words, with a citation:

> "After 28 days, mortality and the numbers of days alive without life support were similar between groups."

My paraphrase: ______________________________________________________________

______________________________________________________________________________

**Check:** different structure? ☐  facts still correct? ☐  no stronger claim than the source? ☐  citation? ☐

## Exercise 3 — Read Paper 1's abstract  *(individual, 12 minutes, segment 2.3)*

Use the **abstract only** of Paper 1: Boulet N, et al. *Crit Care* 2024;28:429 (in `Papers/`). 8 minutes reading, 4 minutes comparing with your neighbour.

**The 15-minute reading order (for later):** title (30 s) → abstract (3 min) → figures & tables (4 min) → methods (5 min) → discussion & limitations (2–3 min). Stop early if the paper does not answer your question.

| Item | What the abstract says |
|---|---|
| **Design** (and blinding) | |
| **P** — who was included? | |
| **I vs C** — what was compared? | |
| **Primary outcome** (and when) | |
| **Numbers** — screened / randomised / analysed | |
| **Main result** — estimate with 95% CI and p | |
| **Conclusion** — one line | |
| Does the conclusion **match** the main result? | ☐ yes ☐ no — why? |
| Any **spin** (words stronger than the numbers)? | ☐ yes ☐ no — where? |
| **Registration** number | |
| Does this paper answer **our** running-example question (28-day mortality)? | ☐ yes ☐ no — why? |

**Fast finishers:** read the **title and abstract** of Paper 2 (Hyun 2023). Which word in the title is stronger than the design allows? Which word does the abstract conclusion use instead?

**Spin checklist — words to look for**

| Data say | Spin says |
|---|---|
| p = 0.42 for the primary outcome | "a non-significant trend" |
| primary outcome: no difference | headline = a positive secondary outcome |
| observational association | "impact", "effect", "reduces" |
| change within one group only | "patients improved" |

## Exercise 4 — Proposal builder 2  *(group, 33 minutes)*

Complete Part 1 of the **Research Proposal template** (`Templates/Research_Proposal_Template.docx`) and the **literature review worksheet**, building on yesterday's question, aim and objectives. This sheet is your checklist.

**Suggested roles:** chair · scribe (types into the template) · searcher (phone or laptop — runs your PubMed string) · timekeeper.

| Time | Task | Done |
|---|---|---|
| 0–8 min | **1. Run your search string** (Exercise 1) in PubMed; write the date, the filters and the number of hits | ☐ |
| 8–16 min | **2. Screen** titles and abstracts; pick **5 key papers**; export them (*Send to → Citation manager*) into Zotero | ☐ |
| 16–22 min | **3. Literature matrix** — one row per paper (split the papers between members) | ☐ |
| 22–28 min | **4. Problem statement** — three short paragraphs (about 300 words): (a) what is known, (b) what is not known — the gap, (c) why it matters *here* (your local number) | ☐ |
| 28–31 min | **5. Working title** and **keywords** (see below) | ☐ |
| 31–33 min | One group reads its title and its gap sentence aloud; the room suggests one improvement | ☐ |

**Working title and keywords**

| | |
|---|---|
| Working title (10–16 words; population, comparison or exposure, and design visible; no abbreviations; no "impact" or "effect" for observational designs) | |
| Number of words | |
| Keywords (3–6; MeSH terms **not** already in the title) | 1. ____________ 2. ____________ 3. ____________ 4. ____________ |

*Example (feasible rewrite of the running example):* "Restrictive versus usual fluids in adults with septic shock: a pilot randomised trial" (13 words). Keywords: Fluid Therapy; Water-Electrolyte Balance; Critical Care; Vasoconstrictor Agents.

**Literature review worksheet — one row per paper**

| # | Study (first author, year, journal) | Design, size | Compared | Primary outcome: result | Key limitation | Why it matters for our question |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | | | | | |
| 2 | | | | | | |
| 3 | | | | | | |
| 4 | | | | | | |
| 5 | | | | | | |

**Search used for the references** (paste the string, the database and the date):

______________________________________________________________________________

**Quality checks before you stop**
- [ ] The problem statement ends with your question; the title names the same population and outcome as the question.
- [ ] At least one reference is a randomised trial or a systematic review, if one exists; you checked a trial registry for ongoing trials.
- [ ] References are saved in a reference manager or exported from PubMed (*Send to → Citation manager*). No sentence is copied from a source.
